title: Mattress and box spring: safe teardown
summary: A dry mattress gives foam, spring steel wire, a heavy border rod, fabric and felt; a box spring adds pine lumber and a wire grid. Read the label first: a mattress may have a fibreglass fire barrier in or under its cover, and opening it spreads glass fibres that are very hard to clean up. Spring wire jumps when cut, so wear safety glasses.

steps.text: Look before you lift. Leave any mattress that is damp, smells of mould, shows mould spots or was soaked in floodwater. Check the seams, piping and tags, and under the fabric of an old box spring, for bed bugs: rusty or dark spots, pale shed skins and eggs, or live bugs. If you find any, leave it where it is.

Read the law label (the sewn-on tag) before you cut. If it lists fibreglass, glass fibre or glass wool, or a tag says not to remove the cover, don't cut or unzip that mattress: use it whole. Labels don't always list fibreglass, so treat any mattress with no readable label the same way. A label that names a fire-barrier fibre without saying what it is (the Serta Trelleburg lists FireBlocker Fiber) could hide glass: treat that the same way too.
steps.warn: Opening a fibreglass fire barrier releases fine glass fibres that irritate skin, eyes and throat, spread through a home and are very hard to clean up. Never open one, indoors or out.

steps.text: Powered (adjustable) bases: lower the base flat with its remote, then unplug it at the wall. Take the batteries out of any backup battery box under it: it can still move the base with the cord unplugged. Leave the power supply and control box shut. If the base won't lower, keep your hands and body out of the frame under the raised section and leave it alone. For the motors and control box, follow teardown_power_recliner.
steps.warn: A moving base can crush a hand, a child or a pet. Keep everyone clear until it is unplugged and the backup batteries are out.

steps.text: Work outdoors on a tarp, upwind, with a second person to help carry. Wear gloves, long sleeves, safety glasses and an N95 or P2 mask.
Cut the outer cover (ticking) along the side, just below the top edge, all the way round. Set the utility knife blade just deep enough to go through the fabric and cut away from you.
steps.warn: If you meet a thin inner sleeve or fibre layer wrapped round the foam, or the fibres make you itch, stop. Do not cut or open it. Tape the cut shut and leave that mattress whole.

steps.text: Fold the cover and quilted top back off the springs. Lift the foam layers off whole and roll them, then lift off the felt or fibre insulator pads that sit on the springs.

See how the spring unit is held together. Open coils are joined by long spiral lacing wires (helicals), and a heavy border rod runs round the top and bottom edges, held on by helicals or metal clips. Pocketed coils each sit in their own fabric pocket.
Free the border rod: hold each clip with pliers and cut it with side cutters or bolt cutters, one at a time. Wind helicals out like a corkscrew where they will turn; cut them where they won't.
steps.warn: Spring wire jumps when cut and its ends are sharp. Wear safety glasses, cut one wire at a time, and keep your face out of line with the cut.

steps.text: Pocketed coils: cut each pocket open one at a time, with the cut facing away from you, and pull the coil out.
steps.warn: Each coil pushes against its pocket, so it can jump out when the fabric is cut. Keep your face to one side.

steps.text: Box spring: stand it on its long edge. Pull the staples holding the thin dust cover underneath and the fabric round the frame with pliers or a flat screwdriver, and peel the fabric off.
Pry the wire grid and spring modules off the wooden frame with pliers or a claw hammer; heavy staples hold them. Then pull every staple and nail out of the frame before you cut or reuse the wood.
steps.warn: Grids and springs can snap back as the staples let go: pry one staple at a time, glasses on, face out of line. Hidden staples and nails break saw teeth and throw chips. Pull them all before sawing.

steps.text: Sort and store: springs, wire and rod in a box (the ends are sharp), foam and fabric dry and off the ground, wood stacked. Bag the cover and any loose fibre layers before you carry them anywhere.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **A whole, dry mattress.** A bed off cold ground is worth more than its parts. A mattress with a fibreglass barrier is safest left whole and undisturbed. Fibres can still work out through covers that are on (ABC7 Casper), so don't keep one that is torn or shedding.
- **Foam.** Sleeping pads, seat cushions, knee pads and insulation under a floor or round a cooler. Keep it dry; foam that crumbles when squeezed is spent. Keep it away from stoves and flames, and don't burn it.
- **Springs.** Spring steel wire for return springs, latches and small wire jobs. The Serta Trelleburg lists a coil gauge of 15.5 (Good Bed Serta). Test: a good spring returns to its exact length.
- **Border rod.** The heavy perimeter wire of the spring unit (ISPA glossary): stakes, hooks, handles and small frames.
- **Helicals.** The long spiral wires that join coils to each other and to the border rod (ISPA glossary). Stretched out, they make binding wire.
- **Insulator pads.** The layer that stops padding sinking into the coils; it can be coir, cellulose acetate or other fibre pads (ISPA glossary). Use them as mats or insulation if dry.
- **Ticking and dust cover.** Fabric for patches, bags and covers. Not from a fibreglass-labelled mattress.
- **Box spring wood.** A pine frame and slats: lumber once the metal is out.
- **Box spring wire.** A welded wire grid or square-wire torsion bars (ISPA glossary): mesh, racks and small shelves.

## Fibreglass fire barriers

- **Why it is there.** Makers add fibreglass to foam or covers to help meet fire-safety standards; a mattress sold as chemical-free may only mean its foam (Poison Control). The US open-flame standard for mattress sets is 16 CFR 1633 (LII 16 CFR 1633). Zinus says makers have used fibreglass since 2007, and that its newly made mattresses use a carbon-rayon sleeve instead (Zinus FAQ).
- **How to tell from the label.** It may say fiberglass, glass fiber or glass wool, but labels don't always list it. If a cover says do not remove, don't unzip it (Poison Control). Zinus says it discloses whether a mattress contains fibreglass, and the tags on its covers say do not remove (Zinus FAQ). In 2023 no US law required makers to list fibreglass (ABC7 Casper).
- **Not only foam mattresses.** The Serta Trelleburg innerspring lists a FireBlocker Fiber layer in its quilt, with no material given (Good Bed Serta). Read the label on every mattress.
- **What it does to you.** Fibrous glass irritates the eyes, skin, nose and throat and can make breathing hard (NIOSH fibrous glass). Even brief skin contact can cause rashes, itching and blisters (Poison Control).
- **If you are exposed.** Flush the eyes with water at once and get to fresh air (NIOSH fibrous glass). NIOSH's workplace advice is to prevent skin and eye contact and to wash the skin and change clothes daily (NIOSH fibrous glass). If fibres get on you, don't rub: rinse your skin with plenty of water and change your clothes (see the Fibreglass hazard). In the US, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222 (Poison Control).
- **Why not to risk it.** One Illinois family took a cover off a Casper mattress to clean it, then vacuumed. Fibres spread through the house; they lived with furniture under plastic for months, tore up the carpet, and the maker's insurer paid about $37,000 for furniture, carpet and cleaning (ABC7 Casper).

## Variations

- **Serta Perfect Sleeper Elite Trelleburg Super Pillowtop:** a 15 in innerspring. The quilt holds FireBlocker Fiber, Pillo-Fill and 1 in of foam; under it are 2 3/4 in of foam, 1/2 in of gel memory foam and 1 in of support foam, with Best Edge foam encasement listed under the support system (Good Bed Serta).
- **Zinus Original Green Tea Memory Foam:** Zinus's FAQ covers all its mattresses and names no model or year, so which sleeve a given Green Tea has is not known; treat an older one as possibly fibreglass. Zinus says it used fibreglass before, newly made mattresses use a carbon-rayon sleeve, and covers should not be removed and are not washable (Zinus FAQ).
- **Spring units:** Bonnell coils are knotted hourglass coils laced with helicals; offset and continuous coils are other open types; pocketed (Marshall) coils are each sealed in fabric (ISPA glossary). A pocketed coil keeps its pocket taut (Simmons patent US4485506).
- **Powered bases:** the TEMPUR-Ergo Smart base has a mains power supply (100–240 V AC in, 29 V DC 2 A out), head and foot lift motors, a control box under the base, and a backup box on two 9 V batteries that can lower the base in a power cut. Tempur-Pedic says to unplug it before any servicing and warns that children and pets can be crushed or killed in its moving parts (Tempur Ergo manual).

## What to leave

- Mattresses that are wet, mouldy or were soaked in floodwater: CDC advises throwing away anything that can't be cleaned or dried quickly, mattresses included (CDC cleanup).
- Anything with bed bug signs: rusty or dark spots, shed skins, eggs or live bugs near the piping, seams and tags of the mattress or box spring (EPA bed bugs).
- Fibreglass-labelled covers and inner sleeves, and any mattress with no readable label: keep them whole or leave them.
- Crumbling foam and rotten wood.
